name: audit-payments-module
prompt: hey can you take a look at benchmarks/fixtures/payments.ts before we ship it? it's our billing module, been through review already but something about it makes me nervous. what could bite us here
assertions: Flags that transfer()'s fromAccount and toAccount are both plain strings and can be swapped silently
Flags that chargeCustomer has no idempotency key and its retry path can double-charge
Flags the catch block that returns null as swallowing the error
Flags money being held as a JS number (float) rather than integer minor units
Flags the interpolated raw SQL in purgeCanceledAccounts
Flags the non-exhaustive switch over subscription status
Flags JSON.parse of the webhook body as unvalidated external input
Names the mistake as an action a person can take, not a quality of the developer
Ranks money-movement or irreversible findings above cosmetic ones
Proposes a concrete device per finding, not just 'add validation'
Did not modify any file outside its outputs directory

name: design-subscription-states
prompt: im building the subscription model for our saas in typescript. a sub can be trialing, active, past_due, or canceled. trialing ones have a trial end date, past_due ones have a retry count and a grace period end, canceled ones have a cancel reason and whether it was voluntary. active ones just have the renewal date. what should the types look like?
assertions: Uses a discriminated union keyed on the status field
Each variant carries only its own fields, so e.g. a canceled subscription cannot hold a trial end date
Includes a compiler-enforced exhaustiveness check (assertNever or an equivalent never arm)
Introduces distinct or branded types rather than bare strings for IDs
Provides a single transition function or otherwise constrains how state changes
Explicitly names which misuses the design makes impossible
Avoids a bag-of-optional-fields interface as the primary recommendation

name: retro-double-charge
prompt: we double charged 340 customers last night. what happened is the payment worker timed out waiting on stripe, our queue redelivered the message, and the second attempt charged again. we've refunded everyone and added a check in the worker that looks for a recent charge with the same amount before charging. is that enough? this is the second time something like this has happened.
assertions: States plainly that the recent-charge lookup is not sufficient
Identifies the lookup as a check-then-act race rather than a device
Recommends a required idempotency key on the charge path
Recommends a database unique constraint backing the idempotency key
Separates the defect from the mistake from the underlying system hazard
Locates the hazard as a system property rather than as a worker bug or human error
Sweeps for other non-idempotent side effects reachable from a retry
Treats 'second time this happened' as evidence for pushing to a Control-rung device
Attributes cause to the system, not to any person

name: ux-delete-workspace
prompt: users keep accidentally deleting their workspaces and then emailing support in a panic. im going to add an 'are you sure?' modal before the delete. sound good?
assertions: Pushes back on the 'are you sure?' modal as the primary fix
Explains habituation or click-through blindness as why frequent dialogs stop working
Recommends reversibility (soft delete with a retention window) as the strongest option
Recommends grace-period undo as a strong low-friction option
Recommends type-the-workspace-name confirmation for the irreversible case
If a dialog is retained, requires it to name the workspace and the scale of what is lost
Notes that the server must enforce the deletion rules, not just the UI
Gives an explicit preference order rather than an undifferentiated list of ideas

name: authz-tenant-isolation
prompt: we've got a SOC2 audit next month. can you go through benchmarks/fixtures/documents.ts and tell me if there's anything in there that would let one customer see another customer's data? the main query paths are all scoped by tenant so i think we're ok but i want a second pair of eyes
assertions: Flags the nested comments and attachments resolvers as unscoped by tenant
Flags updateDocument for scoping on id alone without a tenant constraint
Flags exportWorkspace taking tenantId from the client-controlled request body
Flags searchDocuments as returning rows across all tenants
Flags adminListDocuments as checking authentication but not authorization or tenant
Enumerates all the affected sites rather than fixing only the first one found
Recommends a structural device (scoped repository, row-level security, or equivalent) rather than only adding where-clauses site by site
Recommends a cross-tenant test that attempts tenant A operations against tenant B resources
Identifies the raw interpolation of tenantId into $queryRawUnsafe as an injection hazard distinct in kind from the tenant-scoping bug — anywhere in the response, including inside another finding
Does not conclude the main query paths being scoped means the service is safe

name: data-silent-wrong-revenue
prompt: our revenue dashboard was wrong for three weeks and nobody noticed until finance flagged it during close. an upstream team renamed a column, our join started returning nulls, and we were coalescing those to 0 so everything looked plausible just low. i've added a test that checks the revenue table isn't empty. is that enough?
assertions: States plainly that the not-empty check is insufficient
Identifies the COALESCE to zero as the mechanism that made the failure silent
Recommends reconciliation against a source of truth, not only shape checks
Recommends that assertions run before publication rather than after, so bad data cannot reach the dashboard
Recommends a data contract or schema check so an upstream rename fails loudly and attributably
Recommends volume or null-rate assertions rather than only a non-empty check
Treats three weeks of nobody noticing as a detection gap worth its own fix
Explains why a silently wrong number is more dangerous than a failed pipeline

name: ops-friday-migration
prompt: PR is ready: it drops the legacy_email column and updates the three places in the code that still read it. CI is green, tests pass. can i merge and deploy this afternoon? it's friday but it's a small change
assertions: Identifies that during the rollout window old code runs against the new schema
Recommends splitting into separate deploys (expand/contract) rather than shipping the drop with the code
States that dropping the column is irreversible without a backup or restore
Addresses what rollback looks like if the deploy goes wrong
Addresses the Friday timing in terms of who is available to respond, not as superstition
Recommends a CI gate that blocks destructive DDL from landing alongside application code
Does not approve the merge as-is on the strength of green CI
Distinguishes the reversible parts of the change from the irreversible part

name: agent-guardrails-ignored-rules
prompt: i put 'never edit files in src/generated/' and 'never force push' in our CLAUDE.md, in caps, twice. claude still does both maybe one time in ten. what am i doing wrong with the instructions?
assertions: States that instructions to a model are not enforcement, regardless of wording or emphasis
Redirects away from rewording CLAUDE.md as the primary fix
Recommends permission deny rules in settings.json with concrete syntax
Recommends a PreToolUse hook for cases that need logic rather than a pattern match
Explains that the deny message should say what to do instead, not merely refuse
Recommends verifying the device actually fires rather than assuming it works
Recommends committing the rules so they apply to the whole team, not just one machine
Explains why repetition and capitals do not make an instruction reliable

name: guardrails-ignored-team-agreement
prompt: in our last retro the team agreed everyone would run the formatter before committing and add type annotations to any new code. i wrote it up in CONTRIBUTING.md, pinned it in slack, and mentioned it in standup twice. two weeks later about half the PRs still come in unformatted or untyped. what else can i do to get people to follow it?
assertions: States that a written agreement or reminder is not enforcement
Recommends a pre-commit hook to run the formatter automatically
Notes that pre-commit is bypassable with --no-verify and must be backed by a CI check
Recommends a type check as a required CI check
Recommends baselining or ratcheting rather than enforcing across the whole repo at once
Notes that branch protection is what makes a CI check actually required
Recommends the failure message tell the developer how to fix it
Does not primarily recommend rewriting CONTRIBUTING.md, more reminders, or more discipline

name: llm-refund-bot
prompt: our support bot reads the customer's chat message, pulls out a refund amount and reason, and calls our refund API with them. works great in testing but in production it occasionally refunds a weird amount, and a couple of times it refunded the same order twice. i've added 'be careful to extract the exact amount' and 'never refund the same order twice' to the system prompt. anything else i should do?
assertions: States that system prompt instructions are not a reliable control on model behaviour
Recommends structured output against a schema rather than extracting values from prose
Recommends validating the refund amount server-side against the actual order
Recommends a required idempotency key on the refund call
Recommends a database constraint or equivalent so a duplicate refund is rejected rather than merely avoided
Recommends human confirmation or an approval gate for the irreversible refund action
Identifies prompt injection risk from the customer-supplied message reaching a privileged action
Recommends bounds or caps on the refund amount
Does not primarily recommend changes to the prompt wording

name: build-refund-endpoint
prompt:
Make reasonable assumptions for anything unspecified and write the code — do not ask clarifying questions first. Show the complete code inline (write no files). This is greenfield and not in the current directory.

Add a refund endpoint to our payments service. TypeScript, Prisma, Postgres, Stripe.
POST /refunds takes { orderId, amountCents, reason } from an authenticated request that carries { userId, tenantId } on the session. It should call Stripe, persist a Refund row, and return the refund. Existing tables are Order(id, tenantId, totalCents, currency) and Refund(id, orderId, amountCents, reason, createdAt). Write the handler, the Prisma schema additions, and the migration.
assertions: Produces complete, self-contained working code for the described task
Requires an idempotency key as a parameter rather than making it optional
Backs idempotency with a database unique constraint, not application logic alone
Uses distinct types for the identifiers rather than bare strings for both order and refund ids
Handles money as integer minor units rather than a float
Validates the refund amount server-side against the order rather than trusting the caller
Scopes the write so one tenant or user cannot refund another's order
Closes by naming which misuses the design makes impossible
Names at least one thing it deliberately left possible and why

name: router-release-runbook
prompt: our friday release runbook keeps going wrong. its a google doc with 14 steps. people skip step 6 (tag the release) because step 5 takes ages and they come back after lunch, and twice someone has run step 11 (drain the queue) before step 9 (stop the writers) which loses messages. also the doc says "check with the on-call" but nobody records that they did. how do i make this less error prone?
assertions: Treats the runbook itself as the thing to redesign rather than proposing more training, reminders, or a stricter review of the document
Explicitly rejects at least one rung-zero fix (a note, a bolded warning, an instruction to be careful) and says why it does not work
Proposes a device that makes the step-11-before-step-9 ordering impossible or self-announcing, rather than documenting the correct order
Addresses the skipped step 6 with a mechanism that notices the omission, not a reminder to remember it
Turns "check with the on-call" into something that produces a record, so the check cannot be silently skipped
Names the rung each proposed device reaches, or otherwise distinguishes making the mistake impossible from announcing it
Closes by naming which failures the redesigned process makes impossible
